walkthroughs.body_html:
Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience & Language — a core area of A-Level Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience & Language brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience & Language.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.

Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.

mcqs.q: What are James's four characteristics of mystical experience?
options: Ineffability (beyond words), noetic quality (gives knowledge), transience (temporary), and passivity (feeling acted upon by something greater).
Religious experiences only happen during dreams.
Religious experiences are just hallucinations caused by stress.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.

mcqs.q: What is the problem of evil?
options: If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.
It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.

mcqs.q: How many of Aristotle's causes are there?
options: 2 causes
3 causes
5 causes

mcqs.q: Otto's phrase mysterium tremendum et fascinans describes the numinous as:
options: an awe-inspiring, overwhelming yet fascinating encounter with the 'wholly other'
a peaceful feeling of unity with nature
a logical inference from the order of the universe
a state achievable only through fasting

mcqs.q: Swinburne's principle of credulity states that:
options: we should normally accept that things are as they seem to be, unless we have reason to doubt it
we should never trust reports of religious experience
religious experiences are self-authenticating proofs of God
testimony is only reliable when given by clergy

mcqs.q: Freud regarded religious experience and belief as:
options: an illusion rooted in wish-fulfilment and the longing for a father figure
veridical encounters with the numinous
evidence of the collective unconscious reaching towards God
meaningless noises with no psychological cause

mcqs.q: Religious statements fail Ayer's verification principle because they are:
options: neither analytic nor verifiable by empirical observation
always false as a matter of science
analytic truths about the meaning of 'God'
verifiable only by the clergy

free_texts.hint: Student of Socrates, teacher of Aristotle.
